survey: A park chess table with two stools on grass beside a path. Table: a thick square white top with a blue-and-white checkerboard inset, centred on a single square pedestal. The pedestal stands on a wider square plinth that sits flat on the grass, with a contact shadow. Stools: two white cylinders with slightly flared round seats, one on each side of the table and facing it. Both stand on the grass with contact shadows. The scene is seen in three-quarter view from above, so the board faces the camera at an angle. Every part is a solid cast or stone piece joined in a plain stack (top on pedestal on plinth on ground), which is how real park chess tables are built. There are no cables, hinges or loose parts. Counts are right (one table, two stools on opposite sides), the shapes are consistent (both stool seats are round and the table top is square), and nothing floats or passes through anything else. The checkerboard reads as a regular alternating grid. It is simplified, but the object could stand and work.
